authorisation: Product-Owner mission of 2026-09-24: redesign delivery so normal development is no longer interrupted by the four full CI gates on every push; run one complete authoritative validation each day at 03:10 Africa/Cairo against the exact final HEAD of the active delivery branch; merge automatically on an all-green result and never on anything less. The same mission carries a STANDING PRE-LIVE DEPLOYMENT DECISION and authorises the repository, GitHub Actions, governance, tooling, documentation, commit, push, PR and merge work required to implement it end to end.
what_this_changes_and_what_it_deliberate:
THE COST MOVED; IT DID NOT SHRINK. Measured across a full day of deliveries on 2026-09-23, the four gates cost 29-31 minutes of wall clock on every push, governance was the critical path in every single run (1704-1851s), and QUEUE TIME WAS ZERO -- so none of the wait was GitHub being slow. That is the right price for accepting a change and the wrong price for making one.

NOTHING WAS REMOVED, SHORTENED, OR MADE UNABLE TO FAIL. All four gates still execute in full, with every step they had. What changed is WHEN: once a night, against the one commit actually proposed for master, instead of on every push including the ones about to be superseded.
the_dispatch_is_the_only_mechanism_that_:
A required context is pinned to integration_id 15368 -- the GitHub Actions app -- and branch protection reads the check runs attached to the PULL REQUEST HEAD SHA. That made the two obvious alternatives unavailable rather than merely worse: a schedule-triggered run always runs on the default branch, so its checks attach to MASTER and could never satisfy the pull request; and a commit status posted through the Statuses API carries a different integration, which the pin refuses -- which is exactly what the pin is for. A workflow_dispatch at ref=<delivery branch> produces a run whose head_sha IS the branch tip, so its checks land on the PR head honestly.

THE RULE THAT FORBADE THIS WAS CORRECT WHEN WRITTEN, and it is superseded rather than ignored. It named two real hazards, and both are closed by construction: a dispatched run could block a PR whose own checks were green -- there are now no other checks, the dispatch is the only source of these contexts; and a dispatched success could be inherited as reuse evidence -- the nightly run now DECLINES reuse outright and the orchestrator counts only runs carrying tonight's correlation id. A third hazard the old rule did not name is closed too: a dispatch names a REF, not a commit, so the branch can move between the decision and the checkout. scripts/ci/assert-dispatch-head.sh fails the gate unless the head it is validating is exactly the sha the orchestrator decided on.
the_schedule_is_cairo_semantics_not_a_fr:
GitHub cron is UTC-only and has no timezone support, and Egypt observes DST -- UTC+2 in winter, UTC+3 from the last Friday of April to the last Thursday of October. A single hard-coded UTC cron would therefore be an hour wrong for half the year, which is precisely what the mission forbade.

So the orchestrator fires at BOTH 00:10Z and 01:10Z, and tools/nightly_delivery.py decides which firing is tonight by converting 03:10 Africa/Cairo -- read from the tz database -- back to UTC. Winter: target 01:10Z, so the 00:10Z firing skips as TOO_EARLY. Summer: target 00:10Z, so the 01:10Z firing skips as TOO_LATE. The window is 55 minutes: wide enough to absorb a late scheduler and NARROWER than the one-hour gap between firings, so the wrong firing can never also qualify. Asserted for all 366 nights of a leap year, across both DST transitions, with the measured offsets checked rather than assumed.
fail_closed_behaviour_is_proven_for_all_:
The decision logic is a TESTED MODULE (tools/nightly_delivery.py) rather than inline YAML, because every branch of it can refuse a merge and an `if:` expression cannot be driven through 'what if the PR moved under us'. tools/tests/nightly_delivery/run_negative.py asserts 56 cases, run by the governance gate AND again by the orchestrator itself before it decides anything:

  wrong candidate/head      four green gates for a DIFFERENT sha; a missing expected sha; an abbreviated sha refused because a prefix is not an identity.
  stale nightly PASS        the head re-read after the gates finish and found moved; the head unreadable. A newer commit does not fail -- it waits for the next night.
  missing candidate         none open; only a draft; only a held one; only a non-master base; only closed; no readable head. A quiet no-op, because reporting it as failure would train everyone to ignore the run.
  ambiguous candidates      two and three open at once, refused by name. Choosing between them would invent an intent nobody expressed.
  partial completion        each of the four gates absent in turn; one still in progress; none at all.
  failed gate               failure, cancelled, timed_out, skipped, neutral, action_required, unreported.
  merge without a pass      gates never ran; a gate failed; evidence from a previous night; evidence from a pull_request run.
  schedule/timezone         both DST halves, both cron firings, a 40-minute-late start admitted, a 70-minute-late start refused, and midday refused.

Also asserted: earlier daytime, pull-request, master and PREVIOUS-NIGHT evidence may not substitute; two runs for one gate is refused because which verdict was meant is unknowable; and the live ruleset's own preconditions (unresolved review threads, a branch BEHIND master, mergeable=false, an unknown state) each refuse with a reason instead of producing an opaque 405 at 03:10.

AND THE POSITIVE PATH IS ASSERTED, because a module that refused everything would pass every negative case above and never deliver anything.
why_there_is_a_landing_state:
A GitHub constraint, not a preference: workflow_dispatch only triggers a workflow whose file is on the DEFAULT BRANCH. The delivery that first puts the orchestrator and the gates' dispatch inputs onto master therefore cannot be validated by the mechanism it is adding -- it has to be validated by the pull_request triggers it is about to retire.

So this delivery lands the mechanism with the old triggers still in place and records current_state_facts.delivery_model = NIGHTLY_MODEL_LANDING. The next delivery removes the daytime triggers, flips the field to NIGHTLY_AUTHORITATIVE_VALIDATION, and DELETES the landing value from the validator's accepted set so it can never be used again -- and it is validated and merged BY the new nightly mechanism, which is also the end-to-end proof that the mechanism works.
the_standing_pre_live_deployment_decisio:
Recorded so no future session asks for it again: every completed application/code change may be deployed promptly to PRE-LIVE 172.21.60.25 WITHOUT waiting for the nightly run, until the Product Owner revokes or changes it. It covers build, install, service restart, deployment verification, retry, rollback and exact deployed-source provenance. It authorises no new product, architecture or security decision, no destructive or historical data mutation, no new migration or schema decision, no networking or topology change, no PMS configuration/posting/traffic, no financial or provider activity, no Guest activation or Go-Live, and no Root-CA or trust change.

IT HAS A CONSEQUENCE THAT IS INTENDED RATHER THAN DRIFT: deployed PRE-LIVE source will often be AHEAD of master during the working day. Two rules keep that readable, and the first one has a history -- the deployed-provenance record was wrong immediately after three consecutive deployments, which is why it is updated as PART of deploying rather than afterwards. Always record the exact deployed commit sha read back from the INSTALLED artifact, and never treat deployed PRE-LIVE provenance as authoritative master state: only master records that a change passed the gates.

Written into CLAUDE.md 0F, docs/NIGHTLY_AUTHORITATIVE_DELIVERY.md and current_state_facts.standing_pre_live_deployment_authorization.
a_failed_night_is_preserved_and_picked_u:
Nothing merges, the branch and the failure evidence are preserved, and no gate is re-run by hand. The problem is that NOTHING NOTIFIES ANYONE: the push that caused the failure succeeded, the day ended, and the evidence sits in a workflow run nobody opened. So tools/nightly-status.py is the session-start check, recorded as the first action of every session in CLAUDE.md 0F and in current_state_facts.session_start_check.

It distinguishes UNRESOLVED_FAILURE (exit 1) from CLEAR, IN_PROGRESS and UNKNOWN (exit 2, which is deliberately not the same as clear). 'Unresolved' is not 'the last run was red': a red night followed by fixes is exactly what the model expects, so it is red AND not yet superseded.

the_allow_list_caught_the_model_change_a:
The adversarial mutation suite refuses to run until the GOOD state passes both validators, and it refused: BASELINE FAIL structural=0 keyword=1, which failed the governance gate on the same step as the previous delivery.

THE CAUSE IS A WHITELIST, AND IT IS THE CHECK WORKING. validate-project-state.sh extracts `next authorized (activity|action|step)[^.]*` from both pack files and requires the result to match one of a list of legitimate phrasings; every model change has had to add its own. The nightly model had none. That field is the most visible statement of what an agent may do next, so an unrecognised phrasing means nobody taught the validator what the new state looks like -- which is exactly the condition it should refuse.

This is the SECOND time on this delivery line that this allow-list has caught a model change, and the extractor stopping at the first period is the part that makes it subtle: the captured span here ends at 'PRE-LIVE 172' because the appliance address contains periods. The registered pattern matches the part before that, and the match count in the two pack files was verified as 2 against a minimum of 2.
a_mention_is_not_a_step_and_my_own_comme:
TWO DEFECTS, ONE CAUSE, and it is worth writing down because it is the third instance of the same shape in one session. The four gates carried NEITHER the wrong-commit refusal nor the NIGHTLY_VALIDATION env, while every check reported that they did.

The explanatory comment added above each dispatch trigger names both `assert-dispatch-head.sh` and `NIGHTLY_VALIDATION`. The patcher guarded its inserts with 'is this string already in the file?', the comment answered yes, and it skipped both inserts on all four gates. The validator then asked the same question of the whole file and passed for the same reason. A check and the thing it checks were satisfied by the same sentence.

The earlier two instances this session were the ledger-completeness HEADING standing in for the ledger loop, and a guard that let either of two ledger loops vouch for the other. The lesson that generalises: STRIP COMMENTS BEFORE ASKING WHETHER CODE DOES SOMETHING, and detect a step by its NAME and an env by its exact `KEY:` form -- neither of which prose contains.

PROVEN BOTH WAYS: removing the step while LEAVING the comment now fails with 'does not RUN scripts/ci/assert-dispatch-head.sh in any step', and restoring it passes.

M61 WAS ALSO REPLACED, because it had become OBSOLETE rather than wrong. 'A gate can be satisfied by workflow_dispatch again' encoded the rule this delivery supersedes; under the nightly model a dispatch trigger is the REQUIRED state, so the case reported [MISS] the moment the model landed. An obsolete mutation is worse than no mutation: it fails the suite for the wrong reason and invites someone to 'fix' the validator backwards. Five cases replace it, each removing a protection the new model actually depends on: the head assertion, the reuse refusal, the cron that covers half the year, the orchestrator proving its own rules before merging, and a delivery model nobody enforces.

review_found_two_defects_in_the_one_tool:
Four findings on PR #180. TWO were the defects already fixed at a3174b6f -- the gates carrying neither the head assertion nor NIGHTLY_VALIDATION -- reviewed at the earlier head. The other TWO were new, and both sat in tools/nightly-status.py, which is the only thing standing between a failed night and a session that never hears about it.

P1, THE NEWEST RUN IS NOT NECESSARILY THE ONE THAT DECIDED ANYTHING. The orchestrator fires at 00:10Z and 01:10Z and one firing exits 0 having done nothing. Under EEST the no-op is the LATER of the two, so runs[0] is the no-op -- and the tool would have reported CLEAR while the night's real validation was failing. The tool whose entire purpose is to notice a failure would have been the thing hiding it, every night, for half the year. The orchestrator now prints its verdict and select_authoritative_run() takes the newest run that got past the window guard. An UNREADABLE verdict counts as authoritative on purpose: not being able to read a run must never become a way to skip a red night.

P2, 'RED' IS NOT 'WAITING FOR SOMEBODY', AND MY OWN DOCUMENTATION SAID SO WHILE THE CODE DID NOT. docs/NIGHTLY_AUTHORITATIVE_DELIVERY.md defines unresolved as 'red AND not yet superseded', and the first implementation checked only 'red'. A failure already repaired by a later commit would have gone on telling every future session to stop and fix it. The orchestrator now prints NIGHTLY_TESTED_HEAD and failure_is_unresolved() compares it against the heads currently on offer. An unreadable tested head counts as unresolved, because 'I cannot tell whether this was fixed' is not 'it was fixed'.

BOTH ARE FALSE NEGATIVES -- a tool reporting clear when it is not -- which is precisely the class a suite that only asserts detection cannot catch. Both now live in the tested module and are asserted in both directions: 67 assertions, up from 56.
